reconcile.connective: Commentators distinguish righteous indignation, permitted and even commanded, from the furious, sin-producing wrath the wisdom books and James condemn.

discrepancy.connective: Christopher A. Baba's EvilBible.com presses the plain-sense reading: Ephesians 4:26 flatly approves anger while Ecclesiastes, Proverbs, and James flatly disapprove it.

skeptic.name: Christopher A. Baba
skeptic.work: EvilBible.com, "Is it okay to get angry?"
skeptic.attribution: Christopher A. Baba (editor), EvilBible.com, "Is it okay to get angry?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: Should circumstances arise to call for anger on your part, let it be as Christ's "anger" (Mar 3:5), without sin. Our natural feelings are not wrong when directed to their legitimate object, and when not exceeding due bounds. … Thus indignation at dishonor done to God, and wrong to man, is justifiable anger. Passion is sinful …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes righteous, other-directed indignation from sinful passion, directly reconciling Eph 4:26's permission with the wisdom/James condemnation of anger.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The literal form of the quotation cannot be used to justify anger, for anger gives a foothold to the devil (cp. Jas 1:20). God’s people are to be gentle and gracious, not harsh or angry (see Eph 4:31-32).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly cross-references James 1:20 and argues Ephesians cannot be read as licensing anger, dissolving the apparent conflict rather than merely qualifying it.

excerpts.excerpt_text: We can never suppose that the apostle delivers this as a precept, if we take the words as they stand in our version. Perhaps the sense is, Take heed that ye be not angry, lest ye sin; for it would be very difficult, even for an apostle himself, to be angry and not sin. If we consider anger as implying displeasure simply, then there are a multitude of cases in which a man may be innocently, yea, laudably angry … But, in any other sense, I do not see how the words can be safely taken.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads the KJV wording as a caution rather than a command and restricts sanctioned 'anger' to mere displeasure, aligning it with the wisdom/James condemnations of passionate wrath.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact cluster under the heading "Anger — Approved / Condemned," quoting Eph 4:26, Prov 22:24, Eccl 7:9, and Jas 1:19-20 side by side, then resolves it via Alford and Bishop Butler's distinction between natural, legitimate indignation and cherished, sinful wrath.
